Apple platforms use symbols with no separator, the way menus show them. Windows and Linux use words joined by `+`. Symbols are hard to read aloud, so `spokenKey` gives the name a screen reader should announce instead. <l2/> shows the symbol and puts the spoken name in visually hidden text.

Write each shortcut once, as a string, and use the same string to display it, announce it and match it. `mod` means ⌘ on Apple platforms and Ctrl everywhere else. That's almost always what you want, since Ctrl+K on a Mac and ⌘K on Windows both feel wrong.

`matchesHotkey` checks a keydown event against a hotkey. Modifiers must match exactly, so `mod+b` doesn't fire for `mod+shift+b`.

`parseHotkey` returns one array per chord, with aliases resolved and modifiers sorted into Apple's order: Control, Option, Shift, Command. Every label built from it reads in the order people expect to see it.
`useIsApple()` picks the platform. It returns `true` on the server and during hydration, then the real answer, so a Windows visitor briefly sees ⌘ before Ctrl instead of getting a hydration error.
